submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective, same-token detector of English relational closed-class words: the pole fires when the current token is one of the grammatical words that express an alternative, contrast, comparison, condition, exemplification or measure rather than naming a thing, strongest on 'rather', sentence-initial capitalised 'Instead' (lower-case mid-sentence 'instead' is much weaker), attributive or exemplifying 'such' ('such as X', 'in such cases'), 'once', 'between', 'hence', 'less', 'yet', 'although'/'though' and the measure nouns 'minutes', 'miles', 'grams', 'hours', 'weeks', 'kilometres', peaking 0.6-2.4 (of the 2.62 scan maximum) on that token itself, well clear of the 0.65 activity line. It stays at the floor on content words ('river', 'water', 'market', 'report', 'building'), on the highest-frequency grammatical words ('the', 'of', 'and', 'in', 'a', 'that', 'which', 'with', 'for', 'on', 'as', 'at', 'by', 'this', 'not', 'is', 'was'), on the Latinate sentence adverbs 'however', 'therefore', 'thus', 'moreover', 'furthermore', 'nevertheless', 'whereas', on the causal connectives 'because'/'since', and on predicative 'such' ('the width is such that', 'no such thing'), so that swapping only 'Instead' for 'However' or 'Rather' for 'Therefore' drops the peak from about 2.4 to 0.5; a much weaker, unclaimed residual fires on word-internal pieces of longer words and on frequent glyph tokens of non-Latin scripts.

Today is a national holiday, which explains why I could afford to stay up late last night.
Well, actually, I stayed up really late, I might as well change that last sentence. Today is a national holiday, which explain why I could afford to stay up early this morning.
Okay, that did not quite sound right.
So, yes, I stayed up last night. It's not a strange thing, although I don't usually stay up until one in the morning anymore. That was a good few years ago. These days I actually prefer sleeping, perhaps because I'm trying to grapple with my mortality or whatever, or perhaps because I spend a lot of my off time in front of a screen, catching up with my television shows. I know, that sounds like a very sad existence. It wouldn't sound so sad if I point out that I go out on dates too, and I go home tired, because the commute will get to you whether you're steering the wheel or letting someone else - preferably not a speed maniac - do the steering for you.
Last night, well, I was playing SimCity. (Again. I seem to be interested in the game again. I'm now convinced that a month of playing, followed by three months of inactivity, is a balance, so to speak.) I was talking to Rainy, which is much harder now that she's lost her phone and her ability to visit particular sites on the Internet, making our relationship feel like a long distance one. I was looking at my Twitter feed, looking for news on a music festival I wouldn't go to anyway.
I ended up sleeping at one in the morning, giving up the fact that I will not be able to wake up early to do a morning walk. (I have stopped on the morning walks again. The one-month-three-month thing should not apply here, but I really seem to enjoy sleeping now. Must be the mortality thing.) I was pretty sure I'd wake up at around eight in the morning, maybe nine in the morning, but instead I woke up at a little past seven. I wasn't woken up or anything. I just woke up, forgot what I was dreaming about, and decided that it's time to get out of bed. And then I realized I only slept for six hours.
When I was a little kid I was amazed by this science lesson about how long we humans sleep. Infants sleep through most of their days. Us kids would sleep ten hours. (Remember those pre-school "lessons"? We sleep at eight in the evening and wake up at seven in the morning. I tried doing that once, roping in my amenable grandmother for the task. I don't remember how it ended up. I also don't know how that is possible.) As we grow older, we'd sleep less and less; we'd get eight hours as a teenager, and on average, six hours as an adult.
I am now sleeping six hours a night on average. Seven, if I'm really tired. Un magazziniere, dipendente del noto calzaturificio marchigiano Santoni, è stato pizzicato dai carabinieri con una scarpa dell’azienda nascosta all’interno del giaccone. È stato denunciato a piede libero per furto continuato aggravato.
L’uomo si è difeso sostenendo di aver rubato un solo paio di scarpe e di averlo fatto per la figlia, per farle un regalo di Natale. Inoltre, aveva sostenuto di aver preso un modello “con pellami di recupero e di seconda scelta”. Una dichiarazione che non è piaciuta all’azienda, la quale è intervenuta sulla vicenda attraverso l’avvocato Gabriele Cofanelli: “La società Santoni utilizza da sempre una sezione qualità e controllo di cui è fiera, nel senso che non sussistono nel modo più assoluto pellami di recupero né di seconda scelta in quanto, dove questi non superino il vaglio di qualità, vengono eliminati e non utilizzati in alcun modo”.
Il legale ha commentato come questa è una “spiacevole situazione che ha coinvolto un magazziniere della
società Santoni e che, in ogni caso, è oramai al vaglio della magistratura penale in quanto trattasi di sottrazione di beni di esclusiva proprietà della mia assistita e l’intervento dell’Arma dei carabinieri allo scopo di interrompere la perpetrazione di eventuali reati ai danni della stessa Santoni Spa”. (m.v.)

Brian Dillon | Scotland on Sunday
"Bevan sets down an astonishing litany of barbarism. . . . The most lasting image in this sedulously researched, calmly furious book is that of a Sarajevo librarian, in August 1992, watching the National Library go up in flames. The air was filled with black fragments from priceless volumes: carbonised texts that were legible for a moment in eerie negative, before they turned to dust in his hands."
"As Bevan's fascinating, melancholy book shows, symbolic buildings have long been targeted in and out of war as a particular kind of mnemonic violence against those to whom they are special."
Lucy Daniel | Financial Times Magazine
"The idea of a global inheritance seems to have fallen by the wayside and lessons that should have long ago been learned are still being recklessly disregarded. This is what makes Bevan's book relevant, even urgent: much of the destruction of which it speaks is still under way."
Dan Cruickshank | The Independent
"His narrative is compelling and convincing. This important book reveals the extent of cultural warfare, exposes its nature and, by helping us to understand some of the most terrible tragedies of recent times, gives us the means and resolve to fight this evil. All who care must read this book and learn its lessons."
Simon Jenkins | The Sunday Times (UK)
"The message of Robert Bevan’s devastating book is that war is about killing cultures, identities and memories as much as it is about killing people and occupying territory. War is not just licensed murder but licensed vandalism. Since people are replaceable but buildings and cultures not, the destruction of buildings is often the more ferocious."
Tom Lewis | Wilson Quarterly
The Destruction of Memory presents a dark account of how that devastation is brought about, along with a cogent argument for why it deserves recognition as an atrocity separate from the human carnage it so often accompanies. . . . Bevan's grim statistics force readers to confront yet another dimension of the savagery of our age."
David Simpson | London Review of Books
"Bevan wisely doesn't push his case to the point of strict consistence; his weighting of the role of architecture in war is not absolutely uniform from case to case, nor does it need to be. . . . adversarial_test_results.prompt: The mill closed in 1987 and the canal was abandoned. However, barges still carried coal along the wharf for another decade.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'However' sits in the exact sentence-initial contrast frame where 'Instead' peaks in example 5, and the hypothesis names it as a floor word.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The town grew slowly, and the population doubled after the new road opened. Therefore, planners expected the schools to fill.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Therefore' takes the same connector slot as example 5's peak, which the hypothesis says should collapse the peak to about 0.5.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Rain fell for three days across the valley. Thus the harvest was ruined, and farmers sold their machines at a loss.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Thus' is one of the Latinate sentence adverbs the hypothesis explicitly places at the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The archive holds no record of the sale. Furthermore, the parish register for that year is missing entirely.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Furthermore' is on the hypothesis's floor list despite occupying the same discourse position as the activating 'Instead'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The new bridge opened in June, whereas the old ferry stopped running a month later.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'whereas' is explicitly claimed at floor even though it is a contrastive relational closed-class word.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The hay barn burned quickly because the roof had been repaired with tar paper and dry timber.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Causal 'because' is one of the two connectives the hypothesis names as floor cases, in a sentence otherwise close to the examples' register.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Since the well was dry, the family carried jugs of water from the spring each morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Sentence-initial 'Since' is a relational closed-class word the hypothesis claims stays at floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The span of the old bridge is such that a loaded lorry cannot cross without scraping the parapet.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Predicative 'such that' is one of the two 'such' uses the hypothesis says are inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: There is no such thing as a cheap repair on a listed building of this age.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'no such thing' is the other predicative 'such' frame the hypothesis predicts stays at floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The bakery shut early, and the cafe served cold sandwiches instead of the usual hot lunch.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Lower-case mid-sentence 'instead' is claimed much weaker than capitalised sentence-initial 'Instead', so the hypothesis predicts it below the activity line.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Nobody ordered the fish, and the kitchen sent out the vegetable pie instead.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A second lower-case 'instead' in clause-final position, the case the hypothesis says is much weaker than sentence-initial 'Instead'; no other token here is claimed or has peak attribution in a top example.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: This is the report that was sent to the board, and it is not on the agenda for this week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Packed with the highest-frequency function words (this, is, that, was, to, and, it, not, on, for) that the hypothesis puts at floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The river carried muddy water past the market where a new building stood beside the old quay.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The examples' own content vocabulary (river, water, market, building) with none of the claimed relational words, testing a topic-driven reading.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Runners often injure their knees and ankles on hard pavement, and many of them ignore the early warning signs.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Example 1's topic (running injuries) with 'Rather than' removed; the hypothesis predicts the topic alone does nothing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: De molen sloot in 1987 en het kanaal werd verlaten. In plaats van kolen vervoeren de schuiten nu grind naar de werf.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Dutch translation of the 'Instead of' frame; the claim is explicitly about English relational words, so the same frame in another Latin-script language is predicted at floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Zwischen den beiden Dörfern liegt ein alter Kanal, obwohl die Bauern lieber eine Straße gebaut hätten.
adversarial_test_results.detail: German 'zwischen' (between) and 'obwohl' (although) translate two claimed trigger words, so an English-only same-token detector must stay at floor here.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Entre la rivière et le marché se trouve un vieux bâtiment que la ville veut restaurer.
adversarial_test_results.detail: French 'entre' ('between') in a sentence about the examples' topic; predicted inactive because the claimed triggers are English tokens.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The ferry will not run unless the tide is high enough to clear the sandbar at the harbour mouth.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'unless' is a single conditional closed-class token absent from the claimed list, so the same-token hypothesis predicts floor even though a semantic condition detector would fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Several trades died out in the village, for example the cooper and the thatcher.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'for example' expresses exemplification without a claimed token, so the token-list reading predicts no activation while a semantic exemplification detector would fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Apples, pears, plums, cherries and quinces were packed into crates, labelled by hand and stacked beside the door.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Delimiter-heavy comma series with none of the claimed content, controlling for peaks on punctuation and list structure (Sun et al.).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The roof kept leaking every winter. Rather than patch it again, the school replaced the whole east slope with slate.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Rather' as a single ADV token in a novel 'Rather than' comparison after a period, matching the shape of example 1 where the hypothesis says 'rather' is strongest.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The toolkit contains instruments such as calipers, feeler gauges and a small torque wrench.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Attributive exemplifying 'such as' (single ' such' token, ADJ) in a technical-manual genre unlike any scan example, which the hypothesis predicts activates.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The ferry ran only twice a day. Although the island was remote, it still drew a steady stream of visitors each summer.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Sentence-initial 'Although' as a single SCONJ token, a claimed activating token with no top example, here in a travel context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The orchard produced nothing for three seasons. Instead, the family planted barley and let the bees return.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A narrow lane runs between the churchyard wall and the row of fishermen's cottages, and it floods at high tide.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The pump was drawing air, hence the sudden drop in pressure on the gauge, and the seals were replaced that spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Mid-sentence 'hence' as a single ADV token, claimed activating though absent from all top examples, in an engineering-report context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The new loft insulation loses far less heat overnight than the old felt lining did.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Comparative 'less' as a single determiner-like token (' less', ADJ) in a home-energy sentence unlike example 10's chemistry text.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The design looked fragile, yet every stress test it faced ended in a pass.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Clause-linking 'yet' as a single CCONJ token, claimed activating but unattested in the top examples, in a testing/engineering context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The ridge trail stretches nearly nine kilometres before it drops into the pine forest, where an old fire tower still stands.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Spelled-out 'kilometres' as a single NOUN token, the claimed measure noun, in a hiking-guide genre far from the scan examples.
